title: Feasibility of nurse-delivered alcohol screening and brief intervention on an acute psychiatric ward
subtitle: Feasibility study with pre-stated progression criteria
statement: About a third of adults admitted to a 24-bed acute psychiatric unit drink at harmful levels, but the ward has no routine screening and few patients receive any alcohol intervention before discharge. Before any evaluation of effectiveness, the ward needs to know whether nurses can screen admissions once patients are well enough, whether screen-positive patients accept a two-session brief intervention, whether sessions are delivered as intended on a busy ward, and whether patients can be reached by phone three months after discharge.
whoAffected: Adults admitted to the unit who drink at harmful levels, including people detained under mental health law, their families, and the named nurses who would deliver screening and sessions.
whatHurts: Harmful drinking worsens mental illness, raises the risk of readmission and self-harm, and is rarely addressed during admission; nurses have training they cannot use.
currentPractice: Alcohol use is recorded in the admission notes; there is no screening questionnaire, no ward-based intervention, and referral to the community alcohol team happens for about one patient in ten.
whyNow: Eleven nurses are newly trained, the ward manager has approved protected session time for 2027, and the research office is ready to review a protocol.
constraints: No research nurse: screening and sessions must fit the named nurse's normal shifts. Patients who lack capacity to consent are not approached until capacity returns. Follow-up after discharge is by phone only. Recruitment must finish within nine months.
patientCenteredGoal: Patients who drink at harmful levels are offered help at a moment they find acceptable, without added distress, and leave with a plan they helped make.
summary: Problem framed as a feasibility question about screening, uptake, delivery and follow-up, not about effectiveness.
